titleStmt.title: A Review of Aesthetics, Digital Studies and Bernard Stiegler (2021)

dhq:bio.p: Karel Němeček is a PhD student in the Department of Sociology at Masaryk University. Karel’s research interests include the sociology of finance and digital financial platforms, social theory, environmental and cultural sociology. Previously, Karel completed a Theory of Interactive Media Programme partially focused on Digital Humanities and a thesis on the work of Bernard Stiegler at Masaryk University.

dhq:abstract.p: The edited volume Aesthetics, Digital Studies and Bernard Stiegler develops Digital Studies as a particular approach towards humanities, one which poses questions concerned with the mutual co-creation and co-evolution of human, technical, and social organs. Largely inspired by the work of late French philosopher of technics, Bernard Stiegler, the book explores practical application of his concepts vis-à-vis empirical case studies from a variety of disciplines. While Digital Studies present a broader set of interests than only digital technologies and media, scholars of digital humanities may find inspiration particularly from the Stieglerian post-phenomenological move to treat digital media as escalation of the technological capability to format lifeworlds, enabling usurpation, subjugation, and automatization of basic sensible and intellectual faculties.

dhq:teaser.p: A Review of Aesthetics, Digital Studies and Bernard Stiegler by Fitzpatrick, N., O’Dwyer, N. and O’Hara, M. (eds.) (2021)

body.p: Currently, there are not many anglophone-edited volumes bearing the name of Bernard Stiegler in their title. Thus, Aesthetics, Digital Studies and Bernard Stiegler can clearly entice a reader interested in Stiegler’s philosophy by its mere caption. However, they should not expect a handbook or a critical reception. This is not a Stiegler book first and foremost. Instead, it grew out of a seminar series about the emerging field of Digital Studies . The field is what might make the book particularly enticing to scholars in digital humanities broadly — from arts to philosophy. Digital Studies, instituted by Stiegler, approach digitality as a new mode of being that cuts through all layers of society . That being said, the field does not concern itself only with digitality in a conventional sense, albeit it does not get rid of its particularity either. The Digital in Digital Studies stands for digitus — a finger with which we engage our tools. Thus, it can be understood as an interdisciplinary branch of humanities-based technology studies, characterized by its focus on mutually constituted relationships between technology, humans, their collectives, and exploring the mutual co-creation and co-evolution of human, technical, and social organs . The book aims to define, extend and strengthen this field through a collection of interdisciplinary studies, while firmly affixing itself to Stiegler .

The interpretation that such a conception of the digital destroys the notion of digital humanities as an emerging field would be mistaken. True, digitalized (here, I use digitalized in order to distinguish the digital in the conventional sense from Stiegler’s digital) technologies are, in Stieglerian thought, just another step in a process of grammatization — turning the flow of reality into discrete, reproducible and capturable units enabling us to discern, communicate, engage, expand and transform our lifeworlds . Yet they also present something distinct. Digitalized grammatization formats our consciousness in a uniquely deeper manner. In a post-phenomenological move reminiscent of scholarship on semiocapitalism , digitalized technologies allow us to format not only how we live, produce and consume, but also how we make sense of the world, conceptualize and theorise . In other words, what Stiegler sees as novel with the emergence of digitized technologies and programming industries is the depth to which digital orthography can shape and capture our mental processes . Digitalization changes how we think , as individuals and as collectives . Our very sensibilities and decision-making faculties can now be calculated, automated and subjugated to algorithms . With the advent of digitalization, then, we may ask, for example, how automatized algorithmic processes morph our language conventions, how AI decision-making used in warfare sidesteps our notions of morality, how research engagement with casual forest algorithms impact epistemologies, how digitalization shapes aesthetics, or what cultural forms it enables. By prompting such types of questions, Stieglerian Digital Studies may offer a stimulating engagement and source of inspiration for digital(ized) humanities. Questions of these types are also directly tackled by some of the volume’s authors, such as Connell Vaughan (chapter 6) or Noel Fitzpatrick (chapter 8).

All the editors had either a personal relationship or a collaborative experience with Stiegler — and it shows from the front to back. The book opens with an interview with Stiegler, where he sketches out his philosophy, establishing a foundation for following studies. Similarly, we find a personal note from Fitzpatrick, warmly reminiscing Stiegler, instead of a conclusion. Directly after the opening interview follows an introduction outlining Digital Studies. Acquainted with both Stiegler and Digital Studies, the reader can confidently commence towards individual studies.

The book is split into three sections. Each has an editorial introduction, providing a general insight into a selected concept that connects the subsequent contributions. The section then explores how humanities can be enhanced by digital studies. The first section follows Stiegler’s assertion that technology is a tertiary retention – electronic modes of inscription, which are analyzed here in the light […] that it is technics that give time . This understanding of techno-generated temporality is then applied to a theatre play by Samuel Beckett or used to compare digital and analogue images . Chapters in the second section examine pharmacology — a conceptualisation of technology that simultaneously acknowledges its destructive potential as well as its curative properties. For example, Delaney approaches film criticism through those concepts and explores different ways in which criticism can both numb and enliven the seeing experience [Delaney 2021]. The last section addresses the Negantropocene, Stiegler’s neologism for strategies to reinvent society and change established modes of conduct, primarily to prevent anthropic biosphere destruction. For example, utilization of art can break the habits of mind and behaviour that have formed and are informed through the extreme rationalization of disruption […] . One such rationalization, Putnam shows, is the disruption of landscape by Ireland’s inland border. Artistic landscape photography of Willie Doherty then opens our eyes to the physical reality outside the scope of what is British/Irish . Moreover, while each section is ordained by a unifying concept, concepts are not section-exclusive. Instead, they only correspond with the main emphasis of selected chapters.

I see the organization of sections per concept as a great editorial decision. The chapters cover a great deal of areas, from film studies to hermeneutics. No doubt it could not have been an easy task to find a central organizing principle. The final decision not only provides a logical key, but aids in selecting contributions based on a reader’s interest in Stiegler’s work. Furthermore, the chapters offer new theoretical intersections and empirical applications of Stiegler. For example, Deane analyses how the algorithmic reconstruction of the past is used as legal evidence. He critically connects the notion of technical memory with the concept of control room imaginary, which enchants and heroizes technological remembering and vilifies the human memory . The authors generally perform a good job of explaining Stiegler’s specialized terms and neologisms. The reader should not have an issue in getting the gist of the main ideas after going through the whole book. The pivotal concepts are not only lucid throughout the work, but their practical application can elucidate Stiegler’s thoughts themselves, unburdened with the overarching theoretical apparatus and complicated prose.

That being said, if readers are approaching the book's excerpts without being familiar with Stiegler, they might still struggle. The editors’ and authors’ close knowledge of Stiegler is sometimes taken for granted. Stiegler has been criticized for creating an overly complicated conceptual system closed into itself . While individual contributions attempt to elaborate on Stiegler’s concepts, the language may remain impenetrable to the uninitiated. A glossary would be of tremendous help here. Unfortunately, the book lacks one. Furthermore, while the multidisciplinary contributions certainly open the book to a wider audience, not all chapters immediately indicate their disciplinary affiliation. A short summary of the aims and themes of each chapter within the introduction could certainly render the book more palpable.

Overall, do not expect an introduction to Stiegler. The book is neither a comprehensive excurse into his thinking nor a guide into Stieglerian thought. Other books, such as Howells and Moore’s Stiegler and Technics or Abbinnett’s The Thought of Bernard Stiegler, perform a much better job at that . Rather, the book closely follows Stiegler and expands his project. As such, it may provide guiding points on how to incorporate his ideas into the practice of both digital humanities and classical humanities scholars. It explores Stiegler’s philosophy through the emerging discipline of Digital Studies and offers an inspiration for practical or empirical use of his concepts. Furthermore, it builds up the new discipline and lays a groundwork for Digital Studies’ utilization across disciplines. Unconventionally, the introductory and concluding sections of the book do not address individual contributions all that much. That might complicate usage of the book. Nevertheless, scholars and students already interested in Stiegler or Digital Studies, who would like to make the step from Stiegler’s theories to their application in digital humanities research, have plenty to gain. I have no doubt that this book provides an apt breeding ground for future development in Digital Studies, which stays faithful to its originator — both in spirit and thought.
